To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fluoxetine treatment decreased the gene expression of 5-HTT, proenkephaline, prodynorphine and TH in several brain regions and that these changes were time dependent.

fluoxetine, by inhibiting the uptake of serotonin, produced pronounced and time-related alterations in genes involved the regulation of emotion, suggesting that these changes are involved, at least partly, in the efficacy of this antidepressant.
repeated administration of fluoxetine produced time related alterations in gene expressions of the serotonin, opioid and cannabinoid systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of the action of antidepressants.
the effects of antidepressant drugs on the brain, and the mechanisms by which they produce their effects.

the study of the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation by serotonin of genes involved in emotional behaviour and in the development of new therapeutic strategies for neuropsychiatric disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present study has demonstrated that the time course of the alterations in the expression of genes involved in the control of emotional behaviour induced by fluoxetine in the brain of rat is dependent on the time of administration and on the brain region examined.
the effects of fluoxetine on the brain gene expression are complex and depend upon the brain region and gene studied.

fluoxetine, by inhibiting the uptake of serotonin, produced pronounced and time-related alterations in genes involved, at least partially, in the clinical effects of this drug in the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fluoxetine, by increasing serotonin levels in the brain, produces alterations in gene expressions that are involved in the regulation or emotional behaviour.

fluoxetine, by inhibiting the serotonin reuptake transporter (5-HT transporter) in the brain, induces a series of time-related changes in the expression of genes that code for the serotonin, opioid and cannabinoid systems in the rat brain.

the time related effects of fluoxetine on the transcription of genes encoding for the serotonin transporter and the endogenous opioid and cannabinoid systems are consistent with the hypothesis that the antidepressant-like effect of this drug is mediated, at least in large part, via the serotonergic system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a passive bystander to the effects of antidepressant drugs, but instead, the brain actively adapts and changes in response to these medications.
the brain is not a static organ, it is a dynamic organ.
fluoxetine can be used to treat depression and anxiety disorders, but that it is not effective in treating anxiety disorders that are caused by the presence of a substance abuse disorder.
